Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural primary healthcare clinics
Comments: Equatorial Guinea lacks a national eHealth strategy. WHO SCORE assessment (2013-2018 data) shows low capacity for health service data, with no electronic patient-level data capture in primary care facilities or standardized electronic entry at district level; routine facility reporting scores mostly 0. Bioko Island (not rural mainland) uses DHIS2 for malaria surveillance and digitized patient registries at district hospitals, but field data collection for logistics uses paper forms entered digitally later; transition to Android app ongoing. No evidence of digital patient records (registers, prescriptions) at rural primary clinics; paper-based recording predominant per low HIS capacity and typical sub-Saharan patterns without pilots found.

revision_notes: Original score of 1 (Entirely paper) rested on 2013-2018 WHO SCORE data. A fresh search surfaced Fundación EHAS project documentation (fetched and read), describing a DHIS2-based Health Information System built with Equatorial Guinea's Ministry of Health (MINSABS), Fundación Religiosos para la Salud and the University of Oslo. This replaces the previous fully manual IMA/HIMOD paper-reporting process, and between February and May 2025 went live with direct facility-level digital data entry via the DHIS2 Android app in two districts, including the continental (rural) district of Añisok. This is genuine point-of-service digital capture in at least one rural area, so the code is raised to 2 (Mostly paper - some digital) rather than confirmed at 1. The pilot's limited two-district scope means a higher code is not yet supported.
revised_comments: Data capture in rural primary healthcare clinics in Equatorial Guinea remains predominantly paper-based, though a digital transition is underway. The Ministry of Health and Social Welfare (MINSABS), working with the EHAS Foundation, Fundación Religiosos para la Salud and the University of Oslo, has begun replacing manual monthly activity report sheets (IMA/HIMOD) with a DHIS2-based health information system. Between February and May 2025 a first pilot went live enabling direct digital data entry via the DHIS2 Android app at health facilities in two districts, the coastal Baney and the continental (rural) Añisok, alongside web-based entry at district offices. Outside this pilot, recording across rural clinics continues on paper registration sheets that are periodically collected and transcribed centrally, consistent with the WHO SCORE assessment's finding of low health information system capacity.

Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural police stations
Comments: Extensive searches across targeted queries ("Equatorial Guinea police case management system", "police records paper digital", etc.), US State Dept 2023 Human Rights Report, UK gov.uk guidance, UNODC/World Bank justice reports, and official govt sites (guineaecuatorialpress.com) yield no evidence of digital case management, incident reporting, or records systems for police or gendarmerie (rural force). Criminal record certificates issued manually via Ministry of Justice; processes described as traditional (complaints filed in person). Digital pilots limited to civil registry (World Bank). In francophone-influenced context, rural stations likely use handwritten procès-verbaux. No pilots/donor projects found for police digitalisation; systemic corruption/limited resources noted. Conforms to paper-based norm for rural African police absent contrary evidence.

revision_notes: The cited US State Department 2023 Human Rights Report PDF returned a server error ('technical difficulties/forbidden') on fetch and could not be directly verified. The World Bank ID4D-related document was fetched but concerns the civil registry, not police record-keeping, so it does not directly evidence this variable despite being originally cited. The ENACT Global Organized Crime Index (Africa edition, most recent data) was fetched and confirms very low law enforcement and judicial-system capacity scores for Equatorial Guinea, consistent with paper-based operations, but does not directly describe records digitisation. Fresh searches for police case-management or records digitisation initiatives specific to Equatorial Guinea returned only generic, non-country-specific market-research forecasts (6Wresearch) and unrelated Caribbean deployments (UNDP PRMIS), with no evidence of any actual digitisation project in Equatorial Guinea. In the absence of any authoritative source confirming or contradicting the entirely-paper assessment, the score is confirmed at 1, but this rests on an absence of contrary evidence rather than a direct, dated confirmation.
revised_comments: Rural police stations in Equatorial Guinea are assessed as relying entirely on paper-based case and incident records. No digital case-management, incident-reporting, or records system has been identified for the national police or gendarmerie, and criminal record certificates continue to be issued manually through the Ministry of Justice via in-person processes. The ENACT Organized Crime Index rates Equatorial Guinea's law-enforcement and judicial-system capacity among the weakest in Africa, consistent with an absence of modern records infrastructure, and no donor-funded or government digitisation pilot for policing has been identified, in contrast to the limited civil-registry pilot under way elsewhere in government.

Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural civil registry offices
Comments: UNICEF CRVS profile (2017 data) states that birth, marriage, and death registration in Equatorial Guinea is processed manually on paper at civil registrar’s offices, mayor’s offices, and local authorities. Registration books are sent to central office and filed on paper, with no vital statistics publications or digital systems mentioned. WHO SCORE assessment (2013-2018 data) shows low CRVS capacity (birth registration completeness 53%), no electronic data exchange from local to central levels, and many core attributes missing. A digital civil registry pilot launched in 2018 and commitments to digitization (e.g., Africa CRVS Day 2023), but no evidence of implementation at rural facilities. Rural registry offices likely remain entirely paper-based, consistent with low national digital infrastructure and centralized structure.

revision_notes: Original score of 1 (Entirely paper) rested on a 2017 UNICEF CRVS profile and a 2013-2018 WHO SCORE assessment. Fetched the World Bank's Digital Economy Country Diagnostic (published June 2024) directly; it explicitly confirms the civil registry remains manual and paper-based across all seven regional offices as of 2024, and that the 2018 SIREC pilot (Sistema Informático del Registro Civil, launched by the Ministry of Justice) has not extended to routine facility-level operations. Score confirmed at 1 with a substantially fresher (2024) primary source replacing the 2017 vintage evidence.
revised_comments: Civil registry offices in rural Equatorial Guinea record vital events entirely on paper. The World Bank's 2024 Digital Economy Country Diagnostic confirms the country lacks a unified, digitalised civil registry; instead, seven regional offices each collect and store registration data manually, with completed registers forwarded to a central office for filing and no vital statistics publications produced. A pilot digital civil registry system, SIREC (Sistema Informático del Registro Civil), was launched by the Ministry of Justice in 2018, but this has not extended to routine data capture in rural registry offices, which remain paper-based, consistent with UNICEF's earlier CRVS profile describing a centralised, manual registration process with no electronic exchange between local and central levels.

Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural primary schools
Comments: Rural primary schools in Equatorial Guinea rely entirely on paper-based recording for administrative data, attendance, and learning outcomes. Schools submit physical or basic info sheets annually for the Anuario (statistical yearbook), compiled centrally by the Ministry of Education with PRODEGE support, indicating manual processes at point of service. No evidence found of computers, tablets, or digital tools for daily recording in rural facilities; rural areas suffer electricity shortages (57% no access per 2011 DHS), poor infrastructure, and low resources (textbooks >3:1 ratio). EMIS exists at national level for aggregation (e.g., Rodriguez 2012 evaluation), but data collection remains paper-driven with follow-ups challenging in dispersed rural zones. Recent diagnostics note need for ICT policies and digital skills but confirm limitations in producing digitally skilled population, with no rural point-of-service digitalisation. Barriers: infrastructure deficits, economic crisis, capacity gaps in MEC, incomplete reporting. National ambitions (ADIGE digital agenda) focus on infrastructure/public platforms, not reaching rural school operations; gap evident as central analytics exist but rural reality is manual.

revision_notes: Original score of 1 (Entirely paper) rested on a 2017 World Bank education sector diagnostic. A local news report (dated May 2026) on the official launch of the PRODEGE statistical yearbooks (Anuario) for the 2021-2022 and 2022-2023 school years confirms the underlying data-collection process is still the paper-based Anuario system used for over a decade. A 2025 article on Equatorial Guinea's 2024 Long-Term Strategic Plan describes ambitions to introduce primary-school digital literacy and innovation centres, but frames these explicitly as future reforms, not existing practice. No evidence of any operational digital record-keeping pilot at rural primary-school level was found. Score confirmed at 1 with fresher (2025-2026) corroborating evidence.
revised_comments: Rural primary schools in Equatorial Guinea continue to rely entirely on paper-based administrative and attendance recording. National annual statistics, compiled through the PRODEGE Anuario (most recently the 2021-2022 and 2022-2023 editions, formally launched in May 2026), are gathered via paper information sheets submitted by schools and consolidated centrally by the Ministry of Education, rather than through any point-of-service digital system. The government's Long-Term Strategic Plan, approved in 2024, sets out ambitions to introduce digital literacy from primary level and establish innovation centres, but these remain forward-looking commitments rather than implemented practice, and rural schools continue to lack the electricity access and infrastructure needed for routine digital data capture.
